title: Connie and Carla
full_review:
Two starry-eyed female lounge singers on the lam from gangsters hide out by posing as drag queens in the breezy and brassy but morally muddy comedy, "Connie and Carla" (Universal).

Nia Vardalos and Toni Collette star as Connie and Carla, childhood friends who refuse to give up on their battered dream of making it in show biz. As the film opens we find the struggling songbirds working in a Chicago airport lounge, where they belt out show tunes for snoring patrons.

But when they witness the gangland murder of their boss, Frank (Michael Roberds), by a local kingpin, Rudy (Robert John Burke), the girls go on the run.

Hiding out in Los Angeles, they rent an apartment above a gay bar where they assume new identities as drag queens. Disguised in big-hair wigs and garish glam makeup, they wind up headlining in the bar's nightly live musical revue. Their campy cabaret act becomes an overnight sensation. While they welcome the acclaim that had eluded them for so long, Connie and Carla's song and dance success invites unwanted attention, which ends up leading Rudy right to them.

Much of the film's cross-dressing humor involves the divas trying to keep their secret from their fellow drag queens, many of whom live in the same building and drop by unannounced. Things get really tricky when Connie falls for Jeff (David Duchovny), the nice-guy straight brother of her flamboyantly gay next-door neighbor (Stephen Spinella). The only problem is that Jeff thinks she is a man.

The screenplay (written by Vardalos) borrows elements from several well-known comedies, swiping its on-the-run-from-gangsters premise from Billy Wilder's "Some Like it Hot" (1959), and its gender-bending twist from Blake Edwards' "Victor/Victoria" (1982).

Hot off the success of her sleeper hit "My Big Fat Greek Wedding," Vardalos radiates an almost contagious energy. Ditto for Collette. However, despite their chipper verve, the script drags at times. This is especially true during the film's topsy-turvy climax and the scenes involving Tibor (Boris McGiver), Rudy's Russian leg-breaker who acquires an appreciation for show tunes while scouring dinner theaters across the country in search of the fugitive femmes.

Other off-key elements include a few unnecessarily lewd comments and a puerile parody on piety; after giving Connie and Carla's drab apartment a queer-eye makeover, their gay neighbors light a votive candle and offer a quick petition to "St. Marys, patron saint of drag queens," punctuating the prayer with "gay-men" rather than "amen." In another scene, Connie improvises during a musical number from "Jesus Christ Superstar," opening the door for further irreverence.

"Connie and Carla" also promotes an if-it-makes-you-happy-it's-acceptable kind of morality, which posits a fuzzy felicity as the barometer for gauging the rightness or wrongness of an act or lifestyle.

The infectiously cheerful film touches on issues of identity and femininity while imparting a positive message about self-acceptance and staying true to one's dreams. And though the movie presents a benign attitude toward homosexuality, the farcical context is unlikely to blur the moral outlook of adults.

Still, the film seems to be seeking something more from its viewers than just the recognition of homosexuals as human beings worthy of love and respect. In trying to mend his broken relationship with Robert, it is not enough that Jeff embrace his brother as a person; he must ultimately be supportive of (if not entirely comfortable with) Robert's lifestyle. Jeff's coming out of his closet of supposed "narrow-mindedness" exposes the true teaching objective of the film to be not tolerance, or even compassion, but validation.

Due to a sympathetic portrayal of the gay lifestyle, recurring sexual humor, a sacrilegious comment, an instance of same-sex kissing, intermittent crude language and a few drug references, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
